html:
The Nacotchtank, or Anacostans, were an Algonquian people who lived where Washington, D.C., stands today, along the lower Anacostia River. The river's name comes from theirs.

They were a village people who farmed maize and fished, and traded furs with English merchants from Virginia and Maryland in the early 1600s. Captain John Smith of Jamestown visited them in 1608. They were linked to the Piscataway chiefdom across the Potomac and suffered from raids by the Susquehannock to the north. Disease and English settlement shrank them fast. By the late 1600s the survivors had merged with the Piscataway and moved away, and they vanish from the records.
